PHSCS 587

Polysilicon gate depletion

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how a depleted gate region consumes part of the applied voltage

Treating the gate as an ideal conductor assumes that its internal potential drop is negligible. A doped polysilicon gate can instead develop a depleted region near the oxide under an appropriate bias. That region contains exposed ionized dopants and supports an electric field, adding voltage drop before the field reaches the oxide and semiconductor.

In a simple depletion approximation, the gate-region capacitance per area is Cpoly′ = εSi/Wpoly. Its series contribution gives 1/Ctotal′ = 1/Cpoly′ + 1/Cox′ + 1/Cs′. Wpoly is a bias-dependent gate depletion width in metres, and each C′ is in F/m². A smaller Cpoly′ lowers the incremental gate charge produced by a voltage change and weakens electrostatic control.

Gate depletion differs from depletion in the semiconductor body and from the finite centroid of quantum-confined inversion charge. All can introduce voltage drops, but they arise in different regions and require different models. A sufficiently conductive metal gate removes the particular finite-doped-polysilicon depletion term, while work-function and interface effects still remain.

Example

If a simplified structure has Cpoly′ = Cox′ and an extremely large Cs′, its total capacitance is Cox′/2. With a highly conductive gate, the same oxide-limited structure would instead approach Cox′.

Practice

1. Which physical region produces the extra series term in this lesson?

Locate the depleted layer above the oxide.

The finite-doped polysilicon gate itself develops a depleted region. The body depletion capacitance is a separate term below the oxide.
